opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot. When you run a company at Twitter's scale, almost everything you learn is about managing complexity. You have thousands of people, a product used by hundreds of millions, and a huge amount of existing infrastructure. So the instincts you develop are about process, coordination, risk management, making sure nothing breaks, and getting alignment across many teams before you move. Those are the right instincts in that context. They're survival skills.

At an early-stage company, most of those instincts work against you. At Parallel the biggest risk isn't breaking something that already works. It's building the wrong thing, or building the right thing too slowly. So I've had to consciously stop reaching for the tools that served me well before. I don't need a planning process when I can just talk to the five people who matter. I don't need consensus across stakeholders when the stakeholders are in the same room. And I shouldn't optimize for reliability at a scale we don't have yet.

There's a more subtle part too. At a large company a lot of your job is indirect. You set direction, you hire leaders, you shape the environment, and the work happens through layers of people. At a startup you have to be much closer to the actual work. I'm writing things, debugging things, talking directly to customers, making product calls myself. That shift back into the details took real effort, because the muscle memory says to step back and delegate.

And then there's how you think about the market. At Twitter you're defending and extending something that exists. At Parallel we're building for a world that doesn't fully exist yet, where AI agents are major users of the web. That needs a different kind of conviction. You can't look at the current numbers to tell you you're right. You have to be willing to look a little wrong for a while.

So it's not that the lessons were bad. They were lessons for a different problem, and the hard part is noticing when you're applying them out of habit rather than because they fit.

r001.rationale: The response says Twitter is about defending and extending an existing product while Parallel is building for a world that does not fully exist yet. It does not say Twitter’s development is guided by feedback from existing users.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. The honest answer is that most of what I learned at Twitter was about operating a large company, and almost none of that applies when you're five people in a room trying to figure out if something should exist at all.

At Twitter, so much of the job was about managing a system that already worked. You had hundreds of millions of people using the product, and the question was always: how do we change this without breaking it? You learn to be careful. You learn to think about second-order effects, about how a small change to the timeline ripples through everything. You develop a lot of process around that, and the process is rational for that context. But when I started Parallel, I noticed I was reaching for the same instincts, and they were actively wrong. There was nothing to break. The risk wasn't that we'd damage something valuable; the risk was that we'd move too slowly and never build anything valuable in the first place.

The other thing is how you reason about correctness. At a big company, if you're wrong, there are a lot of mechanisms that catch it. There are other people, there's data, there's review. So you can be decisive in a certain way because the system absorbs mistakes. At a startup, you're often wrong and nobody tells you, because there's no signal yet. You have to build a different relationship with uncertainty. You have to be willing to commit hard to something while knowing you have very little evidence for it, and then be equally willing to throw it away the moment the evidence shows up. That's an uncomfortable posture, and I don't think large-company experience trains you for it at all.

And then there's the AI piece specifically. A lot of my intuitions about distributed systems and infrastructure came from a world where the behavior of the system was deterministic, or close to it. You could reason about it. With models, that's just not true in the same way. You're building on something that's probabilistic, that improves underneath you every few months, and that changes what's possible without you doing anything. So some of the engineering rigor I'm proud of from that era, I've had to loosen, because being precise about a thing that's going to be obsolete in six months isn't rigor, it's just waste.

So the unlearning isn't about the lessons being bad. It's that they were fitted to a very particular situation, and I had to be honest that I'm in a different one now.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts managing Twitter’s established product with figuring out whether Parallel should exist, but it does not say Twitter’s development was guided by existing-user feedback or that Parallel was being built for a customer who had not yet emerged.

astra-6.text:
At Twitter, you were operating inside a system that already existed—a product people used, a business, a large organization. A lot of the work was figuring out how to make changes within those constraints. When you’re building something new, you have to ask which constraints actually exist and which ones you’re bringing with you out of habit.

The temptation is to reach for things you know how to do: introduce a process, define ownership, build a team around a problem. But early on, you may not even understand the problem well enough to do those things. You need to stay close to the work, try something, and be willing to change your mind quickly.

So the unlearning is about recognizing that experience can give you useful instincts, but it can also make you prematurely confident. At Parallel, I want us to earn that confidence through what we build and what we learn from users.

r001.rationale: The response says Twitter already had a product people used and that Parallel is building something new, but it does not say Twitter’s development was guided by existing-user feedback or that Parallel is developing for a customer who has not yet emerged.

sol-6.1.text:
At Twitter, I was operating inside a company that already had a product, hundreds of millions of users, and a lot of history. You could make progress by bringing clarity, coordinating teams, and helping people execute. You also had to think carefully about how any change would affect what was already working.

With Parallel, the uncertainty is much more fundamental. What should we build? What do people actually need? Which of our assumptions are wrong? If you reach too quickly for the tools of running a large organization—process, planning, consensus—you can create the appearance of progress without learning very much.

So the unlearning is about being hands-on again, being willing to do things that don’t scale, and letting a conversation with a customer change what you do tomorrow. The experience is useful, but I have to be careful that it doesn’t become a template I impose on a very different problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes Twitter as an established product with many users and Parallel as a setting of uncertainty and customer discovery. It does not clearly say Twitter’s development was guided by feedback from existing users or that Parallel is being built for a customer who has not yet emerged.
